title: Don't Blame the Scripts
author: Groshell, Zach
summary: This is a transcript of an interview with Naveen Risvi, a UK-based implementer of Direct Instruction programs like Connecting Math Concepts, recorded at the National Direct Instruction Conference where she received the Siegfried Engelmann Excellence in Education Award. Her central argument is that when scripted, evidence-based curricula fail in schools, the failure is almost never the curriculum itself but the conditions surrounding its implementation: inconsistent teacher assignment, insufficient instructional time, absent placement testing, and lack of specialized implementation support (in her case, from NIFDI). She distinguishes 'fidelity' from rigid script-following, defining it instead as deliberately engineering the conditions — trained staff, protected time, correct student placement — that let a program's instructional design actually work as intended. The piece implicitly argues against a common reflex in schools: blaming a program (or by extension, direct instruction as a philosophy) rather than the leadership decisions that starved its implementation of what it needed. It closes on a blunt claim about students who are behind — that only more time plus better instruction, not one alone, can close the gap.
points: Reframes 'fidelity' away from rigid script-reading and toward engineering the real conditions a program needs: one trained teacher, protected instructional time, and accurate placement testing.
Argues that when implementations fail, schools default to blaming the curriculum material itself rather than the leadership and staffing decisions that undermined it.
Documents a concrete failure mode: a program timetabled at half its required minutes, split across four different teachers per week, was doomed regardless of the curriculum's quality.
Closes with a hard claim for anyone designing interventions: kids who are behind need more instructional time AND better instruction — neither alone is sufficient to catch them up.
quotes: What happens in a school environment is that when something goes wrong or you don't have good pre-service or you don't have NIFDI, the program is blamed. It's not the leaders, it's not the lack of training, it's not the lack of placement testing, it's always the books.

With high fidelity, that kind of means committing to conditions that allow the best learning conditions to flourish. So having one teacher, having a teacher who's trained to deliver the program, having somebody who timetables it where the kids have enough hours in a daily session.

The reality is when children are behind nothing's going to help them catch up besides having more time and better instruction. You give them better instruction, but if you don't give them more time, they're not going to catch up.

I've had it without NIFDI. They've had it with NIFDI. And since NIFDI, I've never gone back. And I tell every single school or trust always go with NIFDI because the people that suffer from poor implementation are the kids.

The minute you cut corners on the implementation, you start creating new problems for yourself and those problems are harder to diagnose and then the program gets blamed rather than the conditions that were set for it to thrive in.
